t: Coloring A Border — DFS/BFS on the Component Border
o:
## Understanding the problem

We must find the connected component of same-colored cells containing `grid[row][col]`, then recolor only its **border** cells: cells that touch a cell of a different color (or out-of-grid) in any of the 4 directions.

**Example 1:** `grid = [[1,1],[1,2]]`, start `(0,0)`, color 3. The component is the three 1s. Cell `(0,0)` touches the boundary and cell `(0,1)` touches the 2, so all three cells are border cells → `[[3,3],[3,2]]`.

**Example 3:** `grid = [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]`, start `(1,1)`. Only the outer ring touches the grid boundary; the center `(1,1)` has four same-colored neighbors and isn't on the boundary, so it stays 1 → `[[2,2,2],[2,1,2],[2,2,2]]`.

With `m, n ≤ 50`, even visiting every cell many times is trivially fast, so a straightforward flood fill works.
k: A cell is a border cell iff it lies on the grid edge or has at least one 4-directional neighbor with a different color (or outside the grid).
Flood-fill first to mark the component, then decide border status per cell — this avoids confusion when the new color equals an existing color.
A classic trick: temporarily set visited cells to an invalid sentinel (e.g., negative), then flip border cells to `color` and restore non-border cells to the original color.

a.n: Approach 1: Flood Fill with Visited Matrix
a.i: Run a DFS/BFS from `(row, col)` collecting all cells of the component into a visited set. Then for each collected cell check its 4 neighbors: if any neighbor is out of bounds or has a different original color, it's a border cell and gets recolored. Doing the border check **after** the full fill avoids issues where recoloring mid-traversal changes connectivity decisions.
s: Record `orig = grid[row][col]`; run DFS/BFS marking all reachable same-color cells in a `visited` matrix.
For each visited cell, examine its 4 neighbors.
If a neighbor is out of bounds or `grid[nr][nc] != orig`, mark the current cell as border.
Set every border cell to `color`; leave interior cells unchanged.
a.t: O(m·n) — each cell is visited once by the DFS and checked a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(m·n) — for the visited matrix plus recursion/stack depth up to m·n.

a.n: Approach 2: In-place Sentinel Marking (O(1) extra space)
a.i: Instead of a separate visited matrix, temporarily overwrite component cells with a sentinel value that can't collide (e.g., `-orig`). While filling, we can also detect border cells on the fly: a cell is a border cell if any neighbor is out of bounds or has a value different from `orig` **and** is not a sentinel-marked component cell. After the fill, convert sentinels back: border cells become `color`, others restore to `orig`.
s: Set `orig = grid[row][col]`; negate it as sentinel `s = -orig` (colors are ≥ 1, so no collision).
DFS/BFS: mark current cell as `s`; for each neighbor, if out of bounds or (`grid[nr][nc] != orig` and `grid[nr][nc] != s`), record that the current cell is a border cell.
Second pass: replace every `s` cell with `color` if it was flagged as border, otherwise with `orig`.
a.t: O(m·n) — each cell is marked and restored exactly once.
a.sp: O(m·n) worst case for the recursion/stack; no auxiliary visited matrix (the border flag could be folded into the sentinel encoding for truly O(1) extra beyond traversal).

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it's the cleanest separation of concerns (find component, then classify borders) and easiest to get right. Mention Approach 2's sentinel trick as an optimization if asked about space.

**Pitfalls:**
- Recoloring during the flood fill breaks connectivity checks when `color` equals a neighboring color — always finish the fill before applying the new color.
- Forgetting that grid-boundary cells are automatically border cells even if all their in-grid neighbors match.
- When checking neighbors after negation/sentinel tricks, remember already-visited cells no longer hold `orig`.

**Edge cases:** single-cell grid (always recolored); `color == orig` (answer unchanged but code must still terminate correctly); entire grid one component (everything on the ring recolors, interior doesn't).

**Follow-ups:** What if the grid were huge and sparse? (BFS with a hash set of coordinates.) Can you do it iteratively to avoid stack overflow? (Yes — use an explicit stack/queue, as shown in the JS versions.)
